items.stem: Who wrote "The War of the Worlds" (1898), an early science-fiction novel?
items.answer: H. G. Wells
items.markingKey: H. G. Wells. Wells is a founding figure of the genre.

items.stem: Briefly explain why science-fiction writers often reveal their world gradually.
items.answer: Gradual details let readers discover the world through characters' normal lives, which is more natural and intriguing than long explanations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gradual details let readers discover the world through characters' normal lives, which is more natural and intriguing than long explanations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Science fiction is only about aliens and spaceships." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Much science fiction focuses on human questions – memory, inequality, belonging – using technology as a starting point.
items.markingKey: Much science fiction focuses on human questions – memory, inequality, belonging – using technology as a starting point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction short story.

In 2087 you could sell your memories. Most people sold the boring ones first – queues, commutes, tax forms. The MemoryBank paid well for those; rich people used them to feel ordinary.
Lin sold her seventh birthday to pay the rent.
Afterwards she found a photo of herself in a paper crown, laughing, and felt nothing at all. Not sadness. Not even curiosity.
That was the part the advertisements never mentioned: you didn't miss what you sold. You just became a little less.

Identify the science-fiction conventions in this extract and explain their effect.
items.answer: Science-fiction conventions: a future date (2087), an invented technology (selling memories), a corporation (MemoryBank) and a "what if?" premise used to explore human values.
items.markingKey: Science-fiction conventions: a future date (2087), an invented technology (selling memories), a corporation (MemoryBank) and a "what if?" premise used to explore human values. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction story set on Mars.

The first child born on Mars turned twelve today. Her name is Hope, which everyone agrees was a bit much.
She has never felt rain. She has never seen a dog. When she watches old Earth films, she asks why people walk outside without helmets, as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world.
Tonight she stood at the dome window and pointed at a small blue dot. "Is that really where we're from?" she asked.
Nobody knew how to tell her that it was no longer safe to go back.

Identify the technique used in "it was no longer safe to go back" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Foreshadowing / revelation: "it was no longer safe to go back" – the final line reveals a disaster on Earth, turning curiosity into tragedy.
items.markingKey: Foreshadowing / revelation: "it was no longer safe to go back" – the final line reveals a disaster on Earth, turning curiosity into tragedy. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction short story.

In 2087 you could sell your memories. Most people sold the boring ones first – queues, commutes, tax forms. The MemoryBank paid well for those; rich people used them to feel ordinary.
Lin sold her seventh birthday to pay the rent.
Afterwards she found a photo of herself in a paper crown, laughing, and felt nothing at all. Not sadness. Not even curiosity.
That was the part the advertisements never mentioned: you didn't miss what you sold. You just became a little less.

How does the writer use a science-fiction premise to explore what makes us human?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The futuristic premise – selling memories in 2087 – is built economically through a date, a corporation and a market, and the irony that the rich buy "boring" memories exposes inequality. The flat sentence about Lin selling her seventh birthday makes poverty's cost routine, and the photo she feels "nothing" about shows memory as the basis of feeling. The final metaphor ("a little less") suggests identity itself is being sold.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The futuristic premise – selling memories in 2087 – is built economically through a date, a corporation and a market, and the irony that the rich buy "boring" memories exposes inequality. The flat sentence about Lin selling her seventh birthday makes poverty's cost routine, and the photo she feels "nothing" about shows memory as the basis of feeling. The final metaphor ("a little less") suggests identity itself is being sold. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A genre that imagines the effects of science and technology on society, often set in the future or on other worlds"?
items.answer: science fiction
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of science fiction.

items.stem: Explain the difference between fantasy and science fiction.
items.answer: Science fiction explains its strange elements through science and technology (possible in theory); fantasy uses magic and the supernatural.
items.markingKey: Science fiction explains its strange elements through science and technology (possible in theory); fantasy uses magic and the supernatural. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction short story.

Lin sold her seventh birthday to pay the rent.
Afterwards she found a photo of herself in a paper crown, laughing, and felt nothing at all. Not sadness. Not even curiosity.

Explain how the writer builds a believable world in very few words.
items.answer: World-building is economical: a date, a technology and a market (rich people buy boring memories to "feel ordinary") suggest a whole unequal society in a few sentences.
items.markingKey: World-building is economical: a date, a technology and a market (rich people buy boring memories to "feel ordinary") suggest a whole unequal society in a few sentences. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "Good world-building matters more than characters in science fiction." Discuss.
items.answer: Strong science fiction needs both; the best world-building is revealed through characters whose lives make the world meaningful.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the world makes the genre distinctive; readers enjoy exploring new worlds. Arguments against: readers need characters to care about; world-building is most effective through characters' experience. Supported judgement: Strong science fiction needs both; the best world-building is revealed through characters whose lives make the world meaningful. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Define the term "cautionary tale".
items.answer: A story that warns readers about a danger
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a story that warns readers about a danger. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Science fiction always presents technology as bad." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Science fiction explores both the benefits and dangers of technology; many stories are hopeful or balanced.
items.markingKey: Science fiction explores both the benefits and dangers of technology; many stories are hopeful or balanced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why science fiction is useful for exploring ethical questions.
items.answer: Imagined technologies create situations not yet possible, letting readers test moral questions before they happen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Imagined technologies create situations not yet possible, letting readers test moral questions before they happen. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

How might different readers respond to this advertisement? Explain two possible readings.
items.answer: One reader might see a caring solution to loneliness; a more critical reader might find it sad that a machine replaces human visits, and notice the advert implies families "forget birthdays".
items.markingKey: One reader might see a caring solution to loneliness; a more critical reader might find it sad that a machine replaces human visits, and notice the advert implies families "forget birthdays". Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.answer: Testimonial: ""I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81" – a real-sounding customer makes the product trustworthy and emotional.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Science fiction teaches us more about the present than the future."
items.answer: Science fiction speaks to both, but its greatest value is often in helping readers see present choices more clearly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it exaggerates current trends; its fears reflect its own time. Arguments against: some works predict real technologies; it imagines genuinely new possibilities. Supported judgement: Science fiction speaks to both, but its greatest value is often in helping readers see present choices more clearly.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "the human condition"?
options: The creation of a believable imaginary world, including its technology, society, rules and history
Background information the reader needs to understand the story
The new invention or idea at the heart of a science-fiction story (e.g. selling memories)
The essential experiences of being human – identity, memory, love, mortality, belonging
items.answer: The essential experiences of being human – identity, memory, love, mortality, belonging
items.markingKey: D. "the human condition" is the essential experiences of being human – identity, memory, love, mortality, belonging.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a utopian story and a cautionary tale.
items.answer: A cautionary tale warns of dangers (e.g. technology that erodes identity); a utopian story imagines an ideal society.
items.markingKey: A cautionary tale warns of dangers (e.g. technology that erodes identity); a utopian story imagines an ideal society. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the robot-pet advertisement and the memory story both raise questions about technology and what it means to be human.
items.answer: The robot pet replaces human companionship; the memory market turns identity into a product. Both ask whether technology can replace things that make us human – relationships and memories.
items.markingKey: The robot pet replaces human companionship; the memory market turns identity into a product. Both ask whether technology can replace things that make us human – relationships and memories.

items.stem: "Science fiction is a warning, not a prediction." Discuss with reference to at least one science-fiction text you have read.
items.answer: Indicative content: defines the claim; analyses how a text warns (technology, ethics, human cost); considers predictive elements; judgement. Criteria A and B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: defines the claim; analyses how a text warns (technology, ethics, human cost); considers predictive elements; judgement. Criteria A and B.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "speculative premise".
items.answer: The "what if?" idea at the centre of a speculative story
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the "what if?" idea at the centre of a speculative story. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "A speculative story must be set hundreds of years in the future." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Speculative stories can be set in the near future or an alternative present; what matters is the "what if?" premise.
items.markingKey: Speculative stories can be set in the near future or an alternative present; what matters is the "what if?" premise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a speculative story should focus on one premise.
items.answer: A single strong idea can be explored deeply in a short story; too many inventions confuse readers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single strong idea can be explored deeply in a short story; too many inventions confuse readers. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Image 1: [A photograph: a schoolbag left on a bench at a bus stop in heavy rain; the bus's red tail-lights disappear around the corner.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a crowded night market in Bangkok seen from above; one stall glows brighter than the rest, and a boy stands still in the moving crowd.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a crowd of students marching with hand-painted placards that read "THERE IS NO PLANET B"; one younger girl is on her father's shoulders.]

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]

Using this image as a stimulus, write about 300 words told by a third-person storyteller narrator.
items.answer: Indicative content: a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold; structure – departure – a test in the desert – arrival at dawn; techniques such as imagery of light and darkness, repetition, the oral-storytelling voice; a vast, peaceful and awe-inspiring mood.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a Gothic short story told by a teenage narrator.

My brother says I imagine things. He's probably right. I imagined the scratching behind the wallpaper. I imagined that the mirror in the hall shows the room as it was a hundred years ago – the gas lamps, the dark curtains, the woman in grey.
Last night I imagined she turned round.
This morning there were wet footprints on the stairs. Small ones. Bare.
My brother says I must have walked in my sleep. I didn't tell him that my feet were dry.

Explain the effect of the repetition with irony "I imagined the scratching ... I imagined that the mirror ... Last night I imagined she turned round." on the reader.
items.answer: Repetition with irony: "I imagined the scratching ... I imagined that the mirror ... Last night I imagined she turned round." – the repeated "imagined" seems to dismiss the events, but the growing horror makes the word ironic.
items.markingKey: Repetition with irony: "I imagined the scratching ... I imagined that the mirror ... Last night I imagined she turned round." – the repeated "imagined" seems to dismiss the events, but the growing horror makes the word ironic. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

Read the following extract from a science-fiction short story.

In 2087 you could sell your memories. Most people sold the boring ones first – queues, commutes, tax forms. The MemoryBank paid well for those; rich people used them to feel ordinary.
Lin sold her seventh birthday to pay the rent.
Afterwards she found a photo of herself in a paper crown, laughing, and felt nothing at all. Not sadness. Not even curiosity.
That was the part the advertisements never mentioned: you didn't miss what you sold. You just became a little less.

Write the opening of your own speculative short story (about 300 words) based on a "what if?" question about technology.
items.answer: Indicative content: a clear speculative premise; economical world-building (date, technology, society); a character affected by the technology; a hint of the ethical question; a hook.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a clear speculative premise; economical world-building (date, technology, society); a character affected by the technology; a hint of the ethical question; a hook. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "science fiction"?
options: A genre that imagines the effects of science and technology on society, often set in the future or on other worlds
Computer systems designed to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence
A story that warns readers about a danger
The essential experiences of being human – identity, memory, love, mortality, belonging
items.answer: A genre that imagines the effects of science and technology on society, often set in the future or on other worlds
items.markingKey: A. "science fiction" is a genre that imagines the effects of science and technology on society, often set in the future or on other worlds.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The essential experiences of being human – identity, memory, love, mortality, belonging"?
items.answer: the human condition
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of the human condition.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

Analyse how the phrase "HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY." helps the writer achieve their purpose.
items.answer: Anaphora (repetition): "HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY." – the repeated "never" stresses the robot's advantages over a real pet or busy relatives.
items.markingKey: Anaphora (repetition): "HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY." – the repeated "never" stresses the robot's advantages over a real pet or busy relatives. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Briefly explain why science fiction often comments on the present.
items.answer: Imagined futures exaggerate current trends (inequality, technology, climate) so readers can see them more clearly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Imagined futures exaggerate current trends (inequality, technology, climate) so readers can see them more clearly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why many science-fiction stories are cautionary tales.
items.answer: By showing the harmful consequences of unchecked technology or power, they warn readers about present-day trends.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By showing the harmful consequences of unchecked technology or power, they warn readers about present-day trends. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Noah writes: "Science fiction is only about aliens and spaceships." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Much science fiction focuses on human questions – memory, inequality, belonging – using technology as a starting point.
items.markingKey: Much science fiction focuses on human questions – memory, inequality, belonging – using technology as a starting point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

What does "Companionship, reinvented." suggest about the relationship between humans and machines?
items.answer: Slogan: "Companionship, reinvented." – the short, memorable phrase presents technology as a fresh answer to loneliness.

items.stem: "A speculative story must be set hundreds of years in the future." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Speculative stories can be set in the near future or an alternative present; what matters is the "what if?" premise.
items.markingKey: Speculative stories can be set in the near future or an alternative present; what matters is the "what if?" premise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write three sentences that build a science-fiction world through a character's everyday routine, without explaining the technology directly.
items.answer: Credit details that imply a different world (e.g. "Mira scanned her breakfast for its carbon score before her mother would let her eat it.").
items.markingKey: Credit details that imply a different world (e.g. "Mira scanned her breakfast for its carbon score before her mother would let her eat it.").

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction story set on Mars.

The first child born on Mars turned twelve today. Her name is Hope, which everyone agrees was a bit much.
She has never felt rain. She has never seen a dog. When she watches old Earth films, she asks why people walk outside without helmets, as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world.
Tonight she stood at the dome window and pointed at a small blue dot. "Is that really where we're from?" she asked.
Nobody knew how to tell her that it was no longer safe to go back.

Explain how "as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world" makes the reader think about the effect of technology on people.
items.answer: Dramatic irony / reversal: "as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world" – what is normal for readers is strange for Hope, showing how her world has reversed our assumptions.
items.markingKey: Dramatic irony / reversal: "as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world" – what is normal for readers is strange for Hope, showing how her world has reversed our assumptions. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a robot vacuum cleaner stuck against a door in a dark flat; the door is open just a crack, letting in light.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a crowd of students marching with hand-painted placards that read "THERE IS NO PLANET B"; one younger girl is on her father's shoulders.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a flooded street in a coastal town; a dog sits on the roof of a floating car, looking at the camera.]

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: science fiction story; narrator: a first-person machine narrator; structure: routine – something unusual – the door opens; techniques: an unusual narrator, humour, dramatic irony. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: science fiction story; narrator: a first-person machine narrator; structure: routine – something unusual – the door opens; techniques: an unusual narrator, humour, dramatic irony. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Good world-building matters more than characters in science fiction."
items.answer: Strong science fiction needs both; the best world-building is revealed through characters whose lives make the world meaningful.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the world makes the genre distinctive; readers enjoy exploring new worlds. Arguments against: readers need characters to care about; world-building is most effective through characters' experience. Supported judgement: Strong science fiction needs both; the best world-building is revealed through characters whose lives make the world meaningful.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Science fiction teaches us more about the present than the future."
items.answer: Science fiction speaks to both, but its greatest value is often in helping readers see present choices more clearly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it exaggerates current trends; its fears reflect its own time. Arguments against: some works predict real technologies; it imagines genuinely new possibilities. Supported judgement: Science fiction speaks to both, but its greatest value is often in helping readers see present choices more clearly. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "A speculative story is more effective if the technology is explained scientifically." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Some plausibility helps, but focusing on human consequences is usually more effective than technical explanation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explanation makes it believable; readers enjoy detail. Arguments against: human consequences matter more than mechanics; over-explanation slows the story. Supported judgement: Some plausibility helps, but focusing on human consequences is usually more effective than technical explanation.
